objectives.text: Define business-level strategy and explain how customers (who, what needs, how) shape it
Describe the five generic business-level strategies

publisherSlides.title: Learning Objectives
bullets: Define business-level strategy
Describe the generic strategies
Explain value creation
Evaluate strategy risks

publisherSlides.title: What Is Business-Level Strategy?
bullets: An integrated and coordinated set of commitments and actions
Used to gain a competitive advantage by exploiting core competencies in specific product markets
Answers how the firm will compete, not where it will compete
Every firm needs one for each business it runs
publisherSlides.notes: Contrast with corporate-level strategy, which answers where the firm competes.

publisherSlides.title: Customers: Who, What and How
bullets: Who: which customer groups will we serve
What: which customer needs will we satisfy
How: which core competencies will we use to satisfy those needs
Customer groups can be segmented by demographics, geography, lifestyle and purchase behavior
publisherSlides.notes: Ask students to segment a familiar market before showing the list.

publisherSlides.title: Five Generic Strategies
bullets: Cost leadership
Differentiation
Focused cost leadership
Focused differentiation
Integrated cost leadership and differentiation
The choice depends on competitive scope (broad or narrow) and the source of advantage (cost or uniqueness)
publisherSlides.notes: Draw the 2x2 on the board: scope against source of advantage.

publisherSlides.title: Cost Leadership
bullets: Produce goods or services at the lowest cost relative to rivals
Standardized products for the typical customer in the industry
Relentless efficiency through scale, tight cost control and simple designs
Must still offer acceptable quality and features
Value chain activities: efficient logistics, lean operations and low overhead
Price can match rivals while margins stay higher
publisherSlides.notes: Stress that low cost is not the same as low price.

publisherSlides.title: Cost Leadership and the Five Forces
bullets: Rivals hesitate to compete on price
Powerful buyers can only push prices down to the next most efficient rival
Low costs absorb supplier price increases
Scale deters new entrants
Lower costs protect against substitutes

publisherSlides.title: Differentiation
bullets: Produce goods or services customers perceive as different in ways that matter to them
Customers pay a premium price for unique features
Sources include quality, brand image, service, technology and design
Value chain activities: research and development, marketing and superior service
publisherSlides.notes: The difference must be one customers value enough to pay for.

publisherSlides.title: Focus Strategies
bullets: Serve a narrow segment: a buyer group, a product line or a geographic market
Focused cost leadership: lowest cost within the niche
Focused differentiation: unique value for the niche
Works when broad competitors underserve the niche

publisherSlides.title: Integrated Cost Leadership and Differentiation
bullets: Low cost and some differentiation at the same time
Enabled by flexible manufacturing, information networks and total quality management
Stuck in the middle: neither the lowest cost nor meaningfully different
Requires real capability in both, not a compromise

publisherSlides.title: Risks of Each Strategy
bullets: Cost leadership: technology shifts can erase the cost advantage, and rivals imitate
Differentiation: the price premium grows too large, or customers stop valuing the difference
Focus: broad rivals target the niche, or niche needs converge with the broad market
Integrated: the firm can become stuck in the middle

publisherSlides.title: Chapter Summary
bullets: Business-level strategy is about how to compete
Customers define who, what and how
Five generic strategies
Each strategy carries specific risks

Each activity can lower cost or add something customers value

vignette.workingTitle: Bayshore Marine Supply: chase price or build the service bay?

facts.text: Bayshore Marine Supply is a family-owned marine parts retailer in Clearwater, founded in 1994.
Two big-box marine chains opened stores within 10 miles in 2024.
Gross margin fell from 34% to 27% between 2023 and 2025.
The engine repair department earns a 52% margin and has a three-week waitlist.
facts.source: Your interview with the service manager

facts.text: By March, CEO Dana Whitfield must choose: match big-box prices on commodity parts, or expand repair and specialty parts and stop chasing price.
The company expanded the service bay; revenue recovered to $7.4 million in 2026.

questions.q: Which generic strategy is Pelican Point following today? Use two facts from the case.
questions.analysis: Mostly broad differentiation drifting toward price matching; the margin fall (F4) shows the cost race it cannot win.

questions.q: What is the risk of matching big-box prices on commodity parts?
questions.analysis: Stuck in the middle: the chains have scale (F3), so matching price erodes margin further (F4) without a cost advantage.

questions.q: Recommend a strategy for Jordan Reyes and name the first two value chain changes.
questions.analysis: Focused differentiation around service: repair margin and waitlist (F5) signal valued uniqueness; online sales (F6) stay small.

memo.text: Regional retailers facing big-box entry often respond by matching price, which my field work suggests is the wrong first move.
Generic strategy theory holds that a firm must choose between lower cost and differentiation to sustain an advantage (Porter, 1985).
Resources that are valuable, rare and hard to imitate explain why some firms sustain an advantage (Barney, 1991).
Recent work finds hybrid strategies outperform pure strategies for Gulf Coast retailers (Whitlow & Haines, 2022).
A service-led focus may let a regional firm escape the price war while keeping its customer relationships.
